summary: 1 Kings 21 (29 verses) continues the story of wisdom to idolatry. Starting with 'After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard which was in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.', it moves through themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom and calls readers toward divided kingdom.
whyItMatters: This chapter matters because it shows wisdom to idolatry lived out in solomon to exile. For a first-time reader, it answers: who is God in this moment, what does he ask, and how do people respond.

keyVerses.text: After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard which was in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab king of Samaria.
When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, Jezebel said to Ahab, “Arise, take possession of the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, which he refused to give you for money; for Naboth
“See how Ahab humbles himself before me? Because he humbles himself before me, I will not bring the evil in his days; but I will bring the evil on his house in his son’s day.”

questions.question: What is happening in 1 Kings 21?
questions.answer: In 29 verses, this chapter 1 kings 21 (29 verses) continues the story of wisdom to idolatry. starting with 'after these things, naboth the jezreelite had a vineyard which was in jezreel, next to the palace of ahab king of samaria.', it moves through themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom and calls readers toward divided kingdom. The setting is solomon to exile, written to exiles. Look for who speaks, who listens, and what changes by the end.

questions.question: Who wrote 1 Kings and why 21 matters in the bigger story?
questions.answer: Traditionally prophetic history, addressed to exiles around ~550 bc compiled. This chapter fits the book's purpose as kings history — its themes of wisdom to idolatry, divided kingdom build on what came before.

questions.question: What does 'kingdom' mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: God's reign/ rule. In this chapter, it appears in context of wisdom to idolatry. For a first-time reader: think of it as god's reign/ rule, not just religious jargon.

questions.question: What does this chapter teach about God or people?
questions.answer: Through wisdom to idolatry and divided kingdom, it shows God's character (faithful, just, merciful) and human tendency (need, failure, hope). Notice how verses move from problem to provision.

questions.question: Verse 13 is long — what is it saying in plain English?
questions.answer: The verse says: 'The two men, the wicked fellows, came in and sat before him. The wicked fellows testified against him, even against Naboth, in the presence of the people, saying, “Naboth cursed Go...' In plain terms: it is making a key point about wisdom to idolatry. Break it into two halves — what is described, and what is promised or commanded.

questions.question: How could this chapter apply today without forcing modern ideas onto it?
questions.answer: Ask: what was original audience supposed to do with this? Then ask: what similar situation exists today? For example, if chapter warns about idols, today that might be money or status; if it celebrates deliverance, where do people need deliverance today?
